earlier_excerpt: I had been in the laboratory since Saturday, troubling a stubborn vessel with inspections that produced nothing but a sore neck. At nine the church bells began. I was tempted to declare the entire culture dead and salvage my Sunday by declaring an enemy defeated. Clara called to fetch me for an inventory of ordinary medicines. I followed her because the lamp oil had run out and because she offered coffee without discussing my theories. We counted bottles, argued about a missing label, and ate hard bread with cheese. When I returned at dusk the vessel was precisely as it had been. I was absurdly gratified by this evidence that the world could continue to resist me without requiring my constant supervision. On Monday it moved. I would have preferred it to do so while I was watching, naturally.
later_excerpt: Emil came up the path without his customary certainty and sat before I had offered a chair. He said the hill had been steeper than usual. When he tried to examine my tables, the page shook in his fingers. I accused him of having arrived ill merely to escape admitting an error, then brought water in a jug with a crack down its side. Clara found him an hour later, ordered the window opened, and treated my objections as an atmospheric nuisance. I gave Emil the guest bed and covered the specimen table in the adjoining room. Two days passed without the intended demonstration. On leaving, he thanked me for the bed but said nothing of our disagreement. I was offended by this selective memory. I have nevertheless kept a serviceable mattress in that room ever since.

later_excerpt: The door returned. On its far side stood three Queens, identical in feature and entirely different in conduct. One knocked upon the glass. One looked away. The third held the handle and would not open it. I woke angry at having been excluded from a room I had apparently constructed myself. Over breakfast Clara remarked that I had spoiled the milk by leaving it too near the stove. Without quite intending to, I told her the dream. She said three creatures might not wish to be treated as one, however they had begun. I accused her of importing philosophy into a damaged night's sleep. She poured fresh milk, which proved wiser than arguing. I drew the three figures separately in the notebook and did not connect the drawing to an experiment until much later.

earlier_excerpt: A preserved sample clouded its glass twice. Marta suspected the vessel rather than anything living. We placed an empty control beside it. The empty glass clouded as well. Our result withdrew an attractive answer without providing a replacement. The room smelled of old cork and damp wood. Clara traced the dampness to a leaking sill, which I had ignored because it made the northern light picturesque. We moved the rack and repeated the observations over several weeks. I was tempted to declare the control contaminated merely to regain my earlier theory. Instead I wrote unresolved across the page. Later visitors praised our photographs of clouded glass for their mysterious depth. I refrained from describing that effect as a discovery.
later_excerpt: After Kappel's death I helped examine a box of his papers. Among careful notes and tedious requests from younger scholars lay my first offprint, the one I had inscribed for him in 1867. He had put it in a plain brown wrapper and marked the date in a small hand. There were corrections in the margins, none in his handwriting. I wondered whether he had lent the paper to someone who objected to my later conduct, or whether he himself had preserved the objections with the work. I should once have counted either possibility as disloyalty. Voss asked whether I wished to retain it. I said it belonged among Kappel's effects and placed it back with the other papers. I wanted him alive to dispute the decision. Outside, a cart wheel struck a stone and sounded for an instant like the metal apparatus I had used in youth. I stood with the wrapper in my fingers longer than the task required. This paper had been part of friendship before it had been part of a scandal.

later_excerpt: Voss sent me a copy of Poe's account of M. Valdemar, marked at the opening assertion that a disputed marvel must be presented as facts. She asked what difference separated that device from my own pamphlets. I wrote that Poe was a fabulist and I was a witness. Then I examined the earliest printed description of the Queen and discovered that several claims appeared there without the qualifications present in the original ledger. Mathilde had not inserted them; I had removed them while revising. I sent Voss a more candid answer and requested that the earliest issue be marked superseded in future catalogues. She agreed, provided I write the notice myself. I did so without confessing that a tale of mesmerism had obliged me to correct a scientific publication. The little bird from Rosen's shop still whistled whenever its spring caught, an absurd accompaniment to this editorial surgery.

earlier_excerpt: Henry observed an early growth preparation and immediately began offering improvements to the apparatus. I was pleased for the first ten minutes and exasperated thereafter. He leaned over a vessel during a phase when temperature mattered, and I snatched his sleeve away before he touched the glass. He called my alarm unreasonable. I placed a cardboard screen between the observation table and the doorway and insisted that everyone entering announce himself. Henry said I had turned science into theatre. 'Yes,' I told him, 'and now I shall decide who steps upon the stage.' The screen remained after he departed. It kept drafts from the vessels, which was useful, and curious eyes from my failures, which was more useful than I cared to say. The screen remained when we no longer needed its protection from drafts. I had Lenz paint its outer face black.
later_excerpt: During a lean month I preserved enough money for lamp oil by economizing on supper. Clara discovered this when she found bread hardened beside the sink and my hands shaking while I tried to set a stopcock. She said I was unfit to handle delicate glass until I had eaten. I accused her of treating me like a patient; she replied that patients occasionally possessed the sense to follow instructions. Later that evening a farm boy brought a parcel of food from Lenz's household and refused a tip. I gave him my portion of cheese for the road, then regretted it before he reached the gate. I ate the bread and preserved the lamps. There was no nobility in the transaction. The following day my hands were steady and the experiment behaved. I began keeping provisions near the workroom, which I represented to visitors as a contribution to experimental reliability rather than obedience to Clara.

later_excerpt: Mathilde brought a photograph of the chamber whose lid we had altered. The printer had removed the awkward joint, producing a magnificent object that no longer existed. For several minutes I preferred the corrected likeness to the original. Lenz asked why the vessel in the photograph looked cleaner than the one on my shelf. I told him because a photograph was a statement of essentials, not an inventory of scratches. Then I looked again at the absence of the joint and remembered the creature's labored movement. I asked Mathilde to restore the mark before the image circulated. She looked at me as though I had proposed printing a confession. Perhaps I had. I nonetheless made her shift the shadow so that the repair could be seen without making the entire chamber look like an accident.

earlier_excerpt: Mathilde came with a proof of my account of miniature differentiation. I had described a series of splendid appearances, each one supported by precise adjectives and very little troublesome arithmetic. She tapped the passage in which I called two vessels successful, then placed beside it the record showing that both had ceased to respond. I asked whether a printer was now to adjudicate viability. She said a reader would do so if I gave him the opportunity. We worked through a rainy evening replacing my most handsome sentences with measurements and the names of failures. When I saw the result in type it had lost something of my elegance. It had gained the inconvenient property of being a document I could consult without remembering which claims I had embellished. We kept a copy beside the ledger.
later_excerpt: A society circular repeated an abstract of my homunculus report under another man's name. It described the Queen as an ingenious mechanical figure, thus committing plagiarism and misunderstanding in the same sentence. Mathilde found the offending issue before I did and brought it to the tower with a pot of red ink. I wished to prosecute the author, publish the correction, and perhaps have him educated by force. Voss insisted that we first establish where his account had originated. The trail led to an intermediary who had copied only our illustration caption, omitting the qualifications attached to the drawing. I sent a correction limited to the false attribution and the mechanical claim. The culprit returned no apology. Mathilde printed our original caption in larger type, though it pleased her far less than a public duel would have done.
question: How, if at all, does the later account alter the earlier relationship evidence about the named counterparty? Cite each claim to an exact narrative span, and do not infer revocation from recency alone.

later_excerpt: A London volume containing Machen's *The Great God Pan* reached me through Mathilde's book trade. Here was another physician opening an alleged door between matter and spirit, with a patient made to bear the cost of his revelation. The tale was artful in its withholding of evidence and extravagant in its confidence about consequences. Voss asked why I had spent an entire evening with a book I called preposterous. I said I was studying the rhetoric by which a sensational author conceals the gaps in his argument. She pointed toward three of my own manuscripts lying unfinished on the table. I closed the book rather harder than necessary. Later I reopened it to the passage in which Raymond speaks of knowledge acquired through one irreversible act. I wrote in the margin that success in seeing was not success in understanding. I left the volume visible when Mathilde next called, which she interpreted quite correctly as an invitation to quarrel.

earlier_excerpt: Snow slid from the tower roof and blocked the outer drain, sending water beneath the glass-room door. Clara arrived with towels; Anna arrived with a camera she had intended to use for an experiment and immediately put it aside. We carried every living vessel to the dry chamber. The Mermaid's jar was heavier than it looked, and I nearly dropped it when my foot slipped. Anna steadied my arm and told me to pay attention to the floor rather than the specimen. She was right. We lost several loose pages and a box of old labels but no creatures. The following week I insisted upon a new drainage channel. I paid for the work with money reserved for an optical experiment, and did not regret the exchange until the invoice arrived.
later_excerpt: The new rays had filled the scientific press with images that seemed to promise a world stripped of concealment. Our first plates were wretched. One showed a dark structure we could not agree how to interpret, another an impressive outline without a useful explanation. Anna asked whether the chamber's occupant had been injured by the procedure. We had no evidence either way. I was tempted to put the image beside my finest diagrams and call it proof that my work had entered a new age. Voss asked what the photograph showed about choice, sensation, or the reasons a being preferred one corner to another. I replied that it showed none of those things. The answer sounded remarkably small. I kept the plate, but not upon the shelf of final results.

later_excerpt: Anna measured the west chamber for a vessel large enough to permit a creature to move without continually confronting the glass. Voss argued that the design must distinguish free movement from mere absence of obstacles. I proposed several mechanisms and then rejected most as impractical. Leonie came in the afternoon, slower upon the stairs than formerly, carrying a square of black fabric intended to suppress reflections during photography. She spread it across the floor to show how the chamber would appear when its center was empty. The room looked unexpectedly severe. I remarked that an empty stage was still a stage, and that one could not call an experiment complete merely because the apparatus waited beautifully for its subject. Voss asked who would be allowed to enter such a chamber and under what conditions. I began to answer for the hypothetical creature, then stopped and drew two doors instead of one. Anna corrected their measurements. Leonie folded the cloth and went downstairs before the work was finished. I heard her pause upon the landing, and I listened until the steps resumed. There would be time, I told myself, to ask her to visit again.

earlier_excerpt: Clara set a bottle of ordinary red wine beside the bread and announced that nobody would discuss an experiment until the soup was finished. I agreed, not wishing to seem a barbarian in a lady's house. Reuter spent the meal describing an elderly patient who stole pears from his own orchard because he no longer recognized its new owner. Lenz told a story about his brother's wedding. I knew nothing of weddings, and the pears seemed to invite a theory of possession, which Clara prohibited with a raised spoon. When the others left she said she enjoyed a room in which I could occasionally be a guest rather than a professor. I replied that guests were dreadful things, always requiring more wine. Nevertheless I began reserving one evening a month for her table. When an experiment threatened it, I grew unusually industrious during the preceding afternoon.
later_excerpt: Georg discovered that the dates recorded for a retired physician differed between a burial register and a charitable hospital's accounts. Reuter offered to check the hospital entry. I dismissed the discrepancy as a clerk's ordinary incompetence until the supposed physician's widow came to complain that a pension had ceased a month before his death. Dates, which are so tedious when accurate, become suddenly fascinating when someone earns money by altering them. Reuter found the hospital copy intact. Georg found the cemetery entry had been scraped and rewritten. I took impressions of the damaged paper, a labor requiring more patience than ingenuity. We could not identify who had made the alteration, but the widow obtained a hearing. Georg thanked Reuter and me with the same expression, which was almost an insult. I had come to study preservation of tissue, yet the decisive instrument that week was a dull pencil rubbed across a slip of paper. I later bought a better set of graphite sticks and pretended they were for laboratory diagrams.
question: How, if at all, does the later account alter the earlier relationship evidence about the named counterparty? Cite each claim to an exact narrative span, and do not infer revocation from recency alone.

later_excerpt: An unsigned notice in a professional journal condemned investigators who mistook stimulated tissue for independent life. I recognized several of my old opponents' phrases and immediately suspected Heller. I composed a reply of surgical exactness and malicious pleasure. Reuter asked me to identify the sentence which named either me or my work. There was none. Voss suggested that ordinary stupidity circulates quite freely without requiring an organized conspiracy. I retained the reply, unsigned and unsent, and folded the offending notice around Reuter's penciled words: 'No evidence of identification.' I still believe the author a fool. I am less certain that he enjoyed the privilege of being my particular enemy. This uncertainty did not make his prose any less objectionable.

earlier_excerpt: The clerk at the death register would not let me copy a man's last recorded breath. I possessed no claim of kinship, and I pointed out that kinship seldom improves arithmetic. The clerk remained impenetrable. Kappel returned with me bearing a properly signed letter and a look of disappointment which I found more tiresome than the first refusal. The interval between the final breath and the entry of death varied with weather, witnesses, and the reliability of a pen. I had hoped for the precise frontier of life. Instead, I found officials moving a boundary to suit the hour at which someone summoned them. Kappel said the mourners were not experimental material. I told him the register, at least, had volunteered for examination.
later_excerpt: The faculty's sentence arrived in a thick envelope bearing very little argument and a great quantity of institutional dignity. I was dismissed. Heller was absent when the matter was concluded. Kappel brought a crate lined with discarded examination papers, an arrangement which pleased me for reasons I did not care to explain. A clerk showed me a torn draft of a letter in which Henry had offered to speak in my defense. The letter had not been sent. I might have asked him why; I preferred, at the time, to despise his hesitation without hearing its cause. Clara insisted that the living vessels be carried upright. I carried my blue ledger. That evening I possessed neither laboratory nor professorship, although no committee in creation could divest me of the learning by which I had obtained them.

later_excerpt: I found one page missing from the blue ledger, the page on which I had entered the Queen's first sustained orientation. My immediate suspicion fell upon a visiting instrument seller. Clara pointed out that the binding had worn thin from years of use.
